documents.title: AI Policy for Faculty and Students
documents.summary: Provost policy that leaves AI use to each instructor, requires a syllabus statement, tells students to follow it and to cite AI by default when silent, and urges caution with AI detectors.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'instructors have broad discretion to determine the appropriate use of AI tools in their classrooms' and 'The right to use and the extent of AI tool use for a particular course is at the faculty's discretion', so it sets no stance of its own and hands the decision to instructors. It also 'encourage[s]' responsible use, but only as a general value.

units.why: The preamble says Hofstra 'recognizes the significant contributions and pedagogical value' of AI while noting pitfalls; it frames purpose and principles for the whole policy, so P56 (institution-wide framework), informs.
units.anchor: recognizes the significant contributions and pedagogical value that Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools offer

units.why: 'integral to academic and professional disciplines' gives a career/professional rationale for AI; P44 (AI as professional skill) fits better than P56 because it argues AI belongs in courses.
units.anchor: are integral to academic and professional disciplines and enhance courses and curricula

units.why: 'appropriate ethical use will change over time' says the policy is provisional, so P54 (revisit regularly), phase over-time, informs.
units.anchor: recognition that appropriate ethical use will change over time

units.why: 'Faculty and students are encouraged to use AI responsibly, ensuring transparency, fairness, and respect for privacy' welcomes AI use with conditions, so P02 (permit/encourage by default); the transparency and privacy conditions do not make it P50 or P24, which require specifics.
units.anchor: encouraged to use AI responsibly, ensuring transparency, fairness, and respect for privacy

units.why: 'instructors have broad discretion to determine the appropriate use of AI tools in their classrooms' hands the decision to instructors, so P04, addressed to instructors, before-course, may.
units.anchor: instructors have broad discretion to determine the appropriate use of AI tools in their classrooms

units.why: 'The right to use and the extent of AI tool use for a particular course is at the faculty's discretion' restates that each instructor sets the rule, including 'specific conditions and criteria'; P04, and the course-by-course scope is the point, not P11.
units.anchor: The right to use and the extent of AI tool use for a particular course

units.why: 'The instructor should provide a clear statement about AI utilization in their course syllabus' asks instructors to put an AI statement in the syllabus: P09, should, course-start.
units.anchor: The instructor should provide a clear statement about AI utilization in their course syllabus
units.policy: Instructors provide a clear statement about AI utilization in their course syllabus

units.why: 'respond to any student inquiries on the subject' makes instructors answer students' AI questions. P10 is the nearest type (the ask-the-instructor channel) and P09 does not cover answering questions.
units.anchor: respond to any student inquiries on the subject
units.policy: Instructors respond to any student inquiries about AI use in their course

units.why: 'strongly recommended that the instructor discuss the statement at the course's beginning and as necessary throughout the semester' is about communicating expectations (course-start), so P09 with should.
units.anchor: strongly recommended that the instructor discuss the statement at the course's beginning
units.policy: Instructors discuss the AI statement at the beginning of the course and as necessary throughout the semester

units.why: 'Students must read and abide by any statements in the syllabus regarding AI' binds students to whatever the instructor's syllabus sets; P04 (rule set per instructor) is closest, must.
units.anchor: Students must read and abide by any statements in the syllabus regarding AI
units.policy: Students must read and abide by any statements in the syllabus regarding AI

units.why: 'seek further information from any instructor if needed' tells students to ask when unsure: P10, should (offered as an alternative to reading the syllabus).
units.anchor: seek further information from any instructor if needed
units.policy: Students seek further information from any instructor if needed

units.why: 'If the instructor does not provide guidance, students should cite content derived from AI tools' sets what applies when the syllabus is silent, so P06 rather than P24: the point is the fallback, though it is a citation duty (should).
units.anchor: If the instructor does not provide guidance, students should cite content derived from AI tools
units.frag_start: If the instructor does not provide
units.policy: If the instructor does not provide guidance, students cite content derived from AI tools using the style most closely resembling the course or department's general academic submission format

units.why: 'Please note citation requirements in each course syllabus' points students to syllabus citation rules; P24 (disclose/cite AI use), should.
units.anchor: Please note citation requirements in each course syllabus.
units.policy: Students note the citation requirements in each course syllabus

units.why: 'All final works are the sole responsibility of the student' makes students own what they submit: P29, must.
units.anchor: All final works are the sole responsibility of the student.

units.why: 'AI tools can generate false or biased content' states the factual warning behind verification: P31, informs.
units.anchor: AI tools can generate false or biased content.

units.why: 'essential for students to critically evaluate AI generated content before including it in submitted assignments' requires verification before submission: P31, must.
units.anchor: essential for students to critically evaluate AI generated content before including it in submitted assignments
units.policy: Students critically evaluate AI generated content before including it in submitted assignments

units.why: 'Faculty and students are encouraged to utilize all databases and research tools provided by the Hofstra University Library' recommends vetted, approved institutional tools; P50 (prefer vetted tools) is closest, though these are not AI tools specifically, and P17 requires an AI tool.
units.anchor: approved for use in coursework, unless specified otherwise by an instructor
units.policy: Faculty and students are encouraged to utilize all databases and research tools provided by the Hofstra University Library, which are approved for use in coursework, unless specified otherwise by an instructor

units.why: 'Faculty should exercise caution when using AI detection' warns instructors about detectors: P39 (do not rely on detectors), should, when-misuse.
units.anchor: Faculty should exercise caution when using AI detection.

units.why: 'faculty should not rely on AI detection as the sole source of evidence' limits reliance on detectors because of 'inconsistent accuracy': P39, should-not.
units.anchor: faculty should not rely on AI detection as the sole source of evidence

units.why: 'Faculty Policy Series #11 should be consulted for guidance' sends instructors to the integrity procedure for suspected misconduct: P36 (handled by integrity processes), should.
units.anchor: Faculty Policy Series #11 should be consulted for guidance.
units.policy: Faculty Policy Series #11 is consulted for guidance in cases of suspected academic misconduct

units.why: 'instructors should consider multiple forms of evidence when evaluating potential misuses of AI' tells instructors what to use instead of detectors alone: P40 (process/other evidence), should.
units.anchor: instructors should consider multiple forms of evidence when evaluating potential misuses of AI

units.why: The bulleted list names indicators instructors may weigh as evidence of misuse (writing-style inconsistency, sudden improvement, off-topic content, unusual vocabulary): P40, informs.
units.anchor: Inconsistencies in writing style or quality compared to previous assignments
units.policy: Evidence of possible AI misuse may include inconsistencies in writing style or quality compared to previous assignments, sudden improvements in performance that seem out of character, content that doesn't align with class discussions or materials, responses that don't directly address the assignment prompt, and unusual vocabulary or phrasing for the student's level

documents.title: Resources for Generative AI in Teaching and Learning
documents.summary: Provost EdTech resource page for faculty: definition of generative AI, advice to state expectations, many ideas for redesigning assessments, and links to readings and workshops.
documents.stance_why: The page offers 'faculty resources and recommendations' and says AI use 'must be consistent with the instructor’s stated course policy'; it sets no AI stance and defers to instructors.

units.why: 'Generative AI refers to artificial intelligence or machine learning tools such as ChatGPT or Dall-E 2' defines the term and so the scope of the guidance: P61, informs.
units.anchor: Generative AI refers to artificial intelligence or machine learning tools such as ChatGPT

units.why: 'responses often include inaccuracies' warns that output can be wrong: P31, informs.
units.anchor: responses often include inaccuracies

units.why: 'Your expectations should be clearly communicated with your students' tells instructors to state AI expectations: P09, should, course-start.
units.anchor: Your expectations should be clearly communicated with your students.

units.why: 'the use of generative artificial intelligence tools must be consistent with the instructor’s stated course policy' makes the course policy the governing rule: P04, must.
units.anchor: must be consistent with the instructor’s stated course policy
units.policy: Use of generative artificial intelligence tools must be consistent with the instructor's stated course policy

units.why: 'the ability to discern machine-generated text from human-generated text will diminish' says detection will get harder, which supports P39 (detectors unreliable); informs.
units.anchor: the ability to discern machine-generated text from human-generated text will diminish

units.why: 'paraphrase text, creating additional challenges for text-based detection' names a concrete limit of detection: P39, informs.
units.anchor: creating additional challenges for text-based detection

units.why: 'Start with learning objectives (backwards design)' is an assessment-design tip addressed to instructors: P35, should, before-course.
units.anchor: Start with learning objectives (backwards design)
units.policy: Instructors start with learning objectives (backwards design) when designing assessments

units.why: 'Design assignments that provide opportunities for students to get feedback from you or peers' is an assignment-redesign tip: P35, should.
units.anchor: Design assignments that provide opportunities for students to get feedback from you or peers

units.why: 'Develop a rubric and make it available to students with the assessment' is a design tip about clarity of grading: P35, should.
units.anchor: Develop a rubric and make it available to students with the assessment

units.why: 'Ask students to write a paper that incorporates aspects from the live class discussion' makes assignments depend on class content, a redesign: P35, should.
units.anchor: Ask students to write a paper that incorporates aspects from the live class discussion

units.why: 'Ask students to reflect and share their process by either giving a presentation' with time for questions is a way to check understanding through students explaining their work: P34 over P35 because of the live questions.
units.anchor: Ask students to reflect and share their process by either giving a presentation
units.policy: Instructors ask students to reflect and share their process by giving a presentation or creating multimedia, and build in time for questions from the instructor and other students

units.why: 'Require students to submit written assignments using Google Docs' so revision history makes the process 'transparent': process evidence to identify misuse, P40 rather than P35.
units.anchor: Require students to submit written assignments using Google Docs.

units.why: 'Reflecting on real-life experiences, students can describe their feelings' is a faculty-suggested assignment type that is hard to outsource: P35, informs.
units.anchor: Reflecting on real-life experiences, students can describe their feelings

units.why: 'Relating content with current events' is a faculty-suggested assessment design: P35, informs.
units.anchor: Relating content with current events (e.g. articles)

units.why: 'Expressing their opinions, making predictions, and playing devil’s advocate' is another suggested assignment redesign: P35, informs.
units.anchor: Expressing their opinions, making predictions, and playing devil’s advocate

units.why: 'Asking students to document their process for an assignment' asks for process records (drafts, notes) alongside the work: P26, informs as a suggestion.
units.anchor: Asking students to document their process for an assignment

units.why: 'Giving students options to submit learning artifacts in various formats' is a suggested assessment redesign: P35, informs.
units.anchor: Giving students options to submit learning artifacts in various formats

units.why: 'Commenting on thoughts and discussing any misconceptions they may have in a peer discussion' is a suggested peer-discussion assessment: P35, informs.
units.anchor: discussing any misconceptions they may have in a peer discussion

units.why: 'Ask students to generate an outline and then critique it' is a suggested process-focused assignment: P35, should.
units.anchor: Ask students to generate an outline and then critique it.

units.why: 'Submit a program or line of code then ask students to evaluate the response' suggests an assignment where students critique given code (possibly AI output): P35, should.
units.anchor: Submit a program or line of code then ask students to evaluate the response

units.why: 'A bigger assignment is broken down into smaller pieces so students can submit along the way and receive feedback' is a structural redesign: P35, informs.
units.anchor: A bigger assignment is broken down into smaller pieces

units.why: The page describes a workshop on teaching approaches and tools 'to promote academic honesty'; it supports faculty learning: P63.
units.anchor: this online workshop reviews the teaching approaches and digital tools you can use

units.why: The page offers 'faculty resources and recommendations' and syllabus language for instructors to consider; it supports instructors in setting course policy: P63.
units.anchor: This website offers faculty resources and recommendations to address the use of generative AI tools

documents.title: Syllabus wording: AI prohibited
documents.summary: Provost syllabus wording for instructors who ban AI: no AI or ML tools on any work including exams, treated as unauthorized assistance and an Honor Code violation, with an integrity paragraph and citation links.
documents.stance_why: The template says 'You may not use AI or ML tools, such as ChatGPT or Dall-E, or other similar tools on assignments, discussions, exams, and presentations', and calls use 'a violation of the Hofstra University Honor Code'. It is one syllabus wording for an instructor who chooses prohibition, so I coded the stance of the text itself.

units.why: The shared integrity paragraph says work is done 'entirely and without unauthorized assistance' by the named individual. It binds students on all work, so actor student, phase during-work, must; P29 (own what you submit) fits better than P19 because AI is not named here.
units.anchor: done, entirely and without unauthorized assistance, by the individual(s) whose name(s) it bears

units.why: 'Students bear the ultimate responsibility for implementing the principles of academic integrity' makes students responsible for integrity, which is the P29 ownership idea, as a duty (must).
units.anchor: Students bear the ultimate responsibility for implementing the principles of academic integrity

units.why: 'will not tolerate dishonesty, and it will not offer the privileges of the community to the repeat offender' states consequences escalating by offense, so P37 (penalties stated in advance, escalation) rather than P36, which is about classifying AI misuse.
units.anchor: it will not offer the privileges of the community to the repeat offender
units.frag_start: the University will not tolerate dishonesty

units.why: 'You may not use AI or ML tools, such as ChatGPT or Dall-E' bans AI outright for students in the course: P01, must-not, prohibit.
units.anchor: You may not use AI or ML tools, such as ChatGPT or Dall-E

units.why: The ban extends to 'assignments, discussions, exams, and presentations'; naming exams makes it a P22 unit (during-assessment) alongside the general ban in P01.
units.anchor: assignments, discussions, exams, and presentations in this course
units.policy: No use of AI or ML tools on exams in this course

units.why: 'expected to complete each assignment without assistance from others, including AI/ML automated tools' bars AI from producing or helping with submitted work: P19, must-not.
units.anchor: complete each assignment without assistance from others, including AI/ML automated tools

units.why: Using ChatGPT or similar 'constitutes the receiving of unauthorized assistance' and 'a violation of the Hofstra University Honor Code': AI use is classed as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: is a violation of the Hofstra University Honor Code

units.why: 'See below for resources on citing AI/ML' lists citation guides even in the prohibit template; it points to citation guidance: P24, informs.
units.anchor: See below for resources on citing AI/ML

documents.title: Syllabus wording: AI use with acknowledgement
documents.summary: Provost syllabus wording for instructors who allow AI: use is permitted on all work if it is cited where and how used, with the same integrity paragraph and citation links.
documents.stance_why: The template says 'You may use AI/ML tools such as ChatGPT or Dall-E on assignments, discussions, exams, and presentations in this course if you use clear and accurate citations', so AI is allowed with a disclosure condition. It is one syllabus wording for instructors who choose this option, so I coded the stance of the text itself.

units.why: The shared integrity paragraph says work is done 'entirely and without unauthorized assistance' by the named individual. It binds students on all work, so actor student, phase during-work, must; P29 (own what you submit) fits better than P19 because AI is not named here.
units.anchor: done, entirely and without unauthorized assistance, by the individual(s) whose name(s) it bears

units.why: 'Students bear the ultimate responsibility for implementing the principles of academic integrity' makes students responsible for integrity, which is the P29 ownership idea, as a duty (must).
units.anchor: Students bear the ultimate responsibility for implementing the principles of academic integrity

units.why: 'will not tolerate dishonesty, and it will not offer the privileges of the community to the repeat offender' states consequences escalating by offense, so P37 (penalties stated in advance, escalation) rather than P36, which is about classifying AI misuse.
units.anchor: it will not offer the privileges of the community to the repeat offender
units.frag_start: the University will not tolerate dishonesty

units.why: 'You may use AI/ML tools such as ChatGPT or Dall-E on assignments, discussions, exams, and presentations in this course' allows AI broadly, with a citation condition: P02, may, permit.
units.anchor: You may use AI/ML tools such as ChatGPT or Dall-E on assignments, discussions, exams

units.why: The permission holds only 'if you use clear and accurate citations in the assignment submission where and how AI/ML tools have been used': a disclosure duty with each submission, P24 (the where/how detail is not a separate P27 code-marking rule).
units.anchor: if you use clear and accurate citations in the assignment submission where and how

units.why: 'Any assignment that was completed with AI/ML tools must contain an appropriate citation' repeats the disclosure duty as a flat requirement: P24, must.
units.anchor: Any assignment that was completed with AI/ML tools must contain an appropriate citation.

units.why: 'See below for resources on citing AI/ML' points to citation guides (APA, Penn State, Harper College): P24, informs.
units.anchor: See below for resources on citing AI/ML

notes: Coder B. School and computing layers none-found, course deferred (per collect file). The acknowledgement and prohibited pages are single-option syllabus templates, coded by their own text rather than as delegates; the third template (ai-permission-acknowledgement) was not collected. The P50 unit for library research tools is a loose fit (not AI-specific). The integrity paragraph repeated across both templates is coded in each document.
